A tetrarch was a dependent prince ranking below a king. Luke 3:19–20 has already reported that he imprisoned John the Baptist; John's execution is mentioned in Luke only here, in Herod's own words."},{"verse":14,"phrase":"recline","lemma":"κατακλίνω","kind":"departure","traditional":"sit down","note":"Most English versions say 'sit down'. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for taking one's place at a meal, which was done reclining, and only Luke uses it in the New Testament. Keeping 'recline' lets the scene read as a hosted meal and not merely a seated crowd."},{"verse":20,"phrase":"The Messiah of God","lemma":"Χριστός","kind":"departure","traditional":"The Christ of God","note":"The traditional rendering is 'the Christ of God'. Here the word is a title, God's anointed king whom Israel expected, and not a name, so 'Messiah' conveys what Peter's hearers would have understood. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep 'Christ' where it functions as a name."},{"verse":24,"phrase":"their life","lemma":"ψυχή","kind":"background","traditional":"his life","note":"The Greek word covers both a person's physical life and the person's self; older versions sometimes render it 'soul' in the parallel passages. The saying plays on that range: clinging to one's life loses the self that matters. Verse 25 makes this explicit by replacing the word with 'themselves'."},{"verse":31,"phrase":"his departure","lemma":"ἔξοδος","kind":"background","traditional":"his decease","note":"The Greek word is exodos. It was an ordinary euphemism for death, but it is also the Septuagint's word for Israel's going out from Egypt. With Moses standing in the scene, most interpreters think Luke intends both senses: Jesus' death, resurrection and ascension as a new act of deliverance."},{"verse":32,"phrase":"when they became fully awake","lemma":"διαγρηγορέω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"when they were awake","note":"The verb is rare and can mean either 'wake up fully' or 'stay awake throughout'. On the second reading the disciples fought off sleep and saw the whole event: 'but since they had stayed awake'. Translations are divided, and the context does not settle it."},{"verse":33,"phrase":"three shelters","lemma":"σκηνή","kind":"departure","traditional":"three tabernacles","note":"Older versions have 'tabernacles' and many modern ones 'tents'. The word means a tent or temporary hut, and on a mountainside a shelter of branches is more likely than a tent. Many interpreters see an allusion to the Feast of Booths, when such huts were built, though that is not certain."},{"verse":35,"phrase":"the Chosen One","lemma":"ἐκλέγομαι","kind":"textual","traditional":"my beloved Son","note":"The earliest manuscripts read 'my Son, the Chosen One', which echoes Isaiah 42:1. Most later manuscripts read 'my beloved Son', probably assimilated to the parallel accounts in Matthew and Mark and to the voice at Jesus' baptism. Critical editions and most modern translations follow the earlier reading."},{"verse":41,"phrase":"twisted","lemma":"διαστρέφω","kind":"departure","traditional":"perverse","note":"The traditional rendering is 'perverse', which now tends to suggest sexual deviance. The Greek word means bent out of shape or turned from the right way. The phrase echoes the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:5, where Moses calls Israel a crooked and twisted generation."},{"verse":46,"phrase":"a thought came up among them","lemma":"διαλογισμός","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"an argument arose among them","note":"The Greek word can mean an inward reasoning or an open dispute, and the phrase can be read 'among them' or 'within them'. Most translations have 'an argument arose', in line with Mark 9:34. Since Luke at once says Jesus knew 'the thought of their hearts', using the same word, it is rendered 'thought' in both verses, but an open argument remains possible."},{"verse":51,"phrase":"for him to be taken up","lemma":"ἀνάλημψις","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"that he should be received up","note":"The noun occurs only here in the New Testament. The related verb is used of Jesus' ascension in Acts 1, and most scholars take it here as the ascension, perhaps including the death and resurrection that lead to it. A minority take it simply as a term for his death."},{"verse":53,"phrase":"because his face was set toward Jerusalem","lemma":"","kind":"background","traditional":"because his face was as though he would go to Jerusalem","note":"Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim and rejected the Jerusalem temple, and relations between the two communities were hostile. Pilgrims crossing Samaria on their way to Jerusalem could not count on hospitality. The village's refusal is about the destination, not about Jesus personally."},{"verse":55,"phrase":"But he turned and rebuked them.","lemma":"","kind":"textual","traditional":"But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them.","note":"Many later manuscripts add words of Jesus at the end of verse 55 and the start of verse 56: 'You do not know what kind of spirit you belong to; for the Son of Man did not come to destroy people's lives but to save them.' Some also add 'as Elijah did' to verse 54, making explicit the allusion to 2 Kings 1. The earliest manuscripts lack these words, and critical editions omit them as later additions."}],"candidates":[{"lemma":"ψυχή","rendering":"life","verse":24,"reason":"It ranges over 'life', 'self' and 'soul' across the New Testament, and readers are misled if the same saying appears with 'life' in one Gospel and 'soul' in another."},{"lemma":"ἰδού","rendering":"look","verse":30,"reason":"This very frequent attention marker is variously rendered 'behold', 'look', 'suddenly' or dropped, and a single policy is needed for narrative and speech."},{"lemma":"παραδίδωμι","rendering":"hand over","verse":44,"reason":"Translations alternate between 'betray', 'deliver' and 'hand over' in the passion predictions and the Judas passages, obscuring a deliberate verbal thread."},{"lemma":"ἐπιστάτης","rendering":"Master","verse":33,"reason":"Luke's distinctive form of address to Jesus needs a fixed rendering distinct from those for διδάσκαλος, κύριος and ῥαββί."},{"lemma":"γραμματεύς","rendering":"scribes","verse":22,"reason":"'Scribe' suggests a copyist to modern readers, while the word denotes trained experts in the Law; the choice among 'scribes', 'legal experts' and 'teachers of the law' should be made once."}]}

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Calling the Twelve together, he gave them power and authority over all the demons and to heal diseases,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to cure the sick.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take nothing for the journey: no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, and do not have two tunics apiece.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whatever house you enter, stay there, and leave from there.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And wherever people do not welcome you, as you leave that town shake the dust off your feet as a testimony against them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they set out and went from village to village, bringing the good news and healing everywhere.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was thoroughly perplexed, because it was being said by some that John had been raised from the dead,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the ancient prophets had risen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Herod said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “John I beheaded. Who then is this, about whom I hear such things?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he kept trying to see him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the apostles returned, they told him all that they had done. Then he took them along and withdrew privately to a town called Bethsaida.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the crowds found out and followed him. He welcomed them and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and he cured those who needed healing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The day began to decline, and the Twelve came to him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Send the crowd away so that they can go to the surrounding villages and farms to find lodging and provisions, for we are in a deserted place here.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You give them something to eat.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we ourselves go and buy food for all these people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For there were about five thousand men. He said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Have them recline in groups of about fifty.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They did so and had them all recline.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, blessed them, broke them, and kept giving them to the disciples to set before the crowd.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They all ate and were filled, and what they had left over was collected: twelve baskets of broken pieces.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Once, when he was praying in private and the disciples were with him, he asked them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Who do the crowds say that I am?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “John the Baptist; but others say Elijah, and others that one of the ancient prophets has risen.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “But you—who do you say that I am?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The Messiah of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he gave them a stern warning and ordered them to tell this to no one,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to everyone,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If anyone wants to come after me, they must deny themselves and take up their cross every day and follow me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for my sake, that person will save it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For what good does it do a person to gain the whole world and yet lose or forfeit themselves?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of that person when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you truly, there are some of those standing here who will certainly not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: About eight days after these words, he took Peter and John and James along and went up the mountain to pray.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as he was praying, the appearance of his face became different, and his clothing became white, flashing like lightning.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, two men were talking with him; they were Moses and Elijah,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who appeared in glory and were speaking of his departure, which he was about to fulfill in Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Peter and those with him had been weighed down with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men standing with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Master, it is good for us to be here. Let us make three shelters, one for you, one for Moses and one for Elijah.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did not know what he was saying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was saying this, a cloud came and began to overshadow them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And a voice came from the cloud, saying,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “This is my Son, the Chosen One. Listen to him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. They kept silent, and in those days they told no one anything of what they had seen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a large crowd met him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, a man from the crowd shouted,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, because he is my only child,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and look, a spirit seizes him, and suddenly he screams; it convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and it will hardly leave him, and it is crushing him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I begged your disciples to drive it out, but they could not.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You unbelieving and twisted generation, how long shall I be with you and put up with you? Bring your son here.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While the boy was still approaching, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him violently. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, cured the boy, and gave him back to his father.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all were astounded at the majesty of God. While everyone was marveling at all that he was doing, he said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let these words sink into your ears: the Son of Man is about to be handed over into human hands.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they did not understand this saying. It was veiled from them so that they would not grasp it, and they were afraid to ask him about this saying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then a thought came up among them: which of them might be the greatest?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, knowing the thought of their hearts, took a little child and had the child stand beside him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Whoever welcomes this little child in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me. For the one who is least among all of you, that one is great.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John spoke up and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Master, we saw someone driving out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow along with us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not stop him, for whoever is not against you is for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As the days were being fulfilled for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he sent messengers before his face. They went and entered a Samaritan village to make things ready for him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but the people there did not welcome him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the disciples James and John saw this, they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he turned and rebuked them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they went on to another village.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were going along the road, someone said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I will follow you wherever you go.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Foxes have dens and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To another he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but you, go and announce the kingdom of God everywhere.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yet another said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I will follow you, Lord; but first let me say goodbye to those at my home.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

notes.note: This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome. A tetrarch was a dependent prince ranking below a king. Luke 3:19–20 has already reported that he imprisoned John the Baptist; John's execution is mentioned in Luke only here, in Herod's own words.

Most English versions say 'sit down'. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for taking one's place at a meal, which was done reclining, and only Luke uses it in the New Testament. Keeping 'recline' lets the scene read as a hosted meal and not merely a seated crowd.

The traditional rendering is 'the Christ of God'. Here the word is a title, God's anointed king whom Israel expected, and not a name, so 'Messiah' conveys what Peter's hearers would have understood. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep 'Christ' where it functions as a name.

The Greek word covers both a person's physical life and the person's self; older versions sometimes render it 'soul' in the parallel passages. The saying plays on that range: clinging to one's life loses the self that matters. Verse 25 makes this explicit by replacing the word with 'themselves'.

The Greek word is exodos. It was an ordinary euphemism for death, but it is also the Septuagint's word for Israel's going out from Egypt. With Moses standing in the scene, most interpreters think Luke intends both senses: Jesus' death, resurrection and ascension as a new act of deliverance.

The verb is rare and can mean either 'wake up fully' or 'stay awake throughout'. On the second reading the disciples fought off sleep and saw the whole event: 'but since they had stayed awake'. Translations are divided, and the context does not settle it.

Older versions have 'tabernacles' and many modern ones 'tents'. The word means a tent or temporary hut, and on a mountainside a shelter of branches is more likely than a tent. Many interpreters see an allusion to the Feast of Booths, when such huts were built, though that is not certain.

The earliest manuscripts read 'my Son, the Chosen One', which echoes Isaiah 42:1. Most later manuscripts read 'my beloved Son', probably assimilated to the parallel accounts in Matthew and Mark and to the voice at Jesus' baptism. Critical editions and most modern translations follow the earlier reading.

The traditional rendering is 'perverse', which now tends to suggest sexual deviance. The Greek word means bent out of shape or turned from the right way. The phrase echoes the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:5, where Moses calls Israel a crooked and twisted generation.

notes.phrase: a thought came up among them
notes.note: The Greek word can mean an inward reasoning or an open dispute, and the phrase can be read 'among them' or 'within them'. Most translations have 'an argument arose', in line with Mark 9:34. Since Luke at once says Jesus knew 'the thought of their hearts', using the same word, it is rendered 'thought' in both verses, but an open argument remains possible.

notes.phrase: for him to be taken up
notes.traditional: that he should be received up
notes.note: The noun occurs only here in the New Testament. The related verb is used of Jesus' ascension in Acts 1, and most scholars take it here as the ascension, perhaps including the death and resurrection that lead to it. A minority take it simply as a term for his death.

notes.phrase: because his face was set toward Jerusalem
notes.traditional: because his face was as though he would go to Jerusalem
notes.note: Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim and rejected the Jerusalem temple, and relations between the two communities were hostile. Pilgrims crossing Samaria on their way to Jerusalem could not count on hospitality. The village's refusal is about the destination, not about Jesus personally.

notes.phrase: But he turned and rebuked them.
notes.traditional: But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them.
notes.note: Many later manuscripts add words of Jesus at the end of verse 55 and the start of verse 56: 'You do not know what kind of spirit you belong to; for the Son of Man did not come to destroy people's lives but to save them.' Some also add 'as Elijah did' to verse 54, making explicit the allusion to 2 Kings 1. The earliest manuscripts lack these words, and critical editions omit them as later additions.

candidates.reason: It ranges over 'life', 'self' and 'soul' across the New Testament, and readers are misled if the same saying appears with 'life' in one Gospel and 'soul' in another.
This very frequent attention marker is variously rendered 'behold', 'look', 'suddenly' or dropped, and a single policy is needed for narrative and speech.
Translations alternate between 'betray', 'deliver' and 'hand over' in the passion predictions and the Judas passages, obscuring a deliberate verbal thread.
Luke's distinctive form of address to Jesus needs a fixed rendering distinct from those for διδάσκαλος, κύριος and ῥαββί.
'Scribe' suggests a copyist to modern readers, while the word denotes trained experts in the Law; the choice among 'scribes', 'legal experts' and 'teachers of the law' should be made once.
